video_title: Luke Burgis on Mimetic Desire, Catholicism, and the Age of Social Contagion
gist: Luke Burgis (author of Wanting and The One and the Ninety-Nine, founder of the Cluny Institute) argues to Tyler Cowen that AI will make social contagion weaker, not stronger, by moving the West from an 'age of information' to an 'age of intelligence' of personalized, autodidactic learning. He predicts the pope's forthcoming AI encyclical will be optimistic against tech-world expectations, explains why he declined an unpaid Anthropic invitation to comment on Claude's constitution as reputational cover, calls efficient markets theory 'BS' from his Wall Street years, and lays out a mimetic framework for herding, false contrarianism, algorithmic gender sorting, and long-horizon institution-building.

themes.theme: AI, anti-mimetics, and the AI-ethics credibility economy

insights.claim: Luke Burgis predicts AI will make social contagion weaker rather than stronger, because the West is leaving the 'age of information' and entering an 'age of intelligence' in which individuals follow their own intellectual threads instead of the crowd's.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Directly contrarian to the consensus that AI amplifies herding; if right, it argues against a permanent regime of algorithm-driven narrative synchronization and for products that serve individual discovery rather than feed-based virality.
insights.quote: I would bet that it’s going to make social contagion weaker.

insights.claim: Burgis frames personalized AI tutoring and self-directed learning as fundamentally non-mimetic processes, because a user following footnotes and obscure sources through an AI is pursuing their own interests rather than copying a crowd.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that personalized-education and research-assistant AI products have durable demand distinct from social/attention platforms, whose economics depend on the contagion Burgis expects to weaken.
insights.quote: Because we’re leaving the age of information and entering what I would call the age of intelligence.

insights.claim: Burgis argues AI is performing a 'via negativa' on the human person by stripping away what is not distinctively human, which he expects to trigger a renaissance in the humanities rather than their decline.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A demand-side case for humanities-adjacent goods (meaning, liturgy, ritual, in-person community, credentialing of taste) as AI commoditizes analytic output; watch for capital flowing toward experience and identity products, not just automation.
insights.quote: I think AI is performing a kind of via negativa on the human person, maybe even the human soul, in helping us discover who we are.

insights.claim: Burgis says he uses AI mainly to surface the cross-domain implications of his own writing that his blind spots hide, describing the output as consistently surprising.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A concrete high-value use case (implication mapping across unfamiliar domains) for knowledge-worker AI tooling, distinct from drafting or summarization, and a hint at where willingness-to-pay is real.

insights.claim: Burgis expects AI to rapidly change the form of the written word itself, including the traditional essay, invoking Marshall McLuhan's medium-shapes-message framing without predicting where it lands.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Format risk for text-native publishing and subscription-essay businesses; the unit of consumption, not just the cost of production, may be repriced.
insights.quote: the traditional forms of written word, even traditional essays, that is changing incredibly fast in the world that we’re entering

insights.claim: Burgis declined an unpaid Anthropic invitation that brought roughly 14 or 15 people — he says all Christians interested in virtue ethics — to San Francisco for a couple of days to comment on Claude's constitution, because he suspected the exercise was reputational positioning rather than genuine inquiry.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Concrete detail on how a leading AI lab sources external moral legitimacy; a signal that unpaid 'ethics consultation' formats are starting to face credibility pushback from the very advisors they recruit.
insights.quote: flying out to San Francisco to consult for Anthropic for free is not one of them

insights.claim: Burgis says the Anthropic outreach was framed to him as a moral imperative — by lab staff and by fellow Christians who know him — which he treats as a warning sign rather than a reason to participate.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Moral-imperative framing is a recruiting and legitimacy tool in AI; watch for a backlash cycle in which unpaid advisory labor and 'we consulted the ethicists' claims lose signaling value.
insights.quote: It was framed like a moral imperative, not only by people at Anthropic, but even by people that know me, by fellow Christians.

insights.claim: Burgis argues AI labs' discovery of virtue ethics and 'discernment' is a rediscovery of what Ignatius and the Jesuits worked out 500 years ago, and that nobody could answer his question of what comes after the two-day consultation.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Suggests the intellectual moat in AI alignment/values work is thinner than marketed and that existing religious-ethical traditions are an underused, cheap input — a possible arbitrage for labs and for advisors who can bridge them.

insights.claim: Burgis judges effective altruism to have largely failed at its own aims because 'effectiveness' is never pinned down and its measurement bias excludes relationships, depth, and culture.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: EA has shaped AI-lab governance and philanthropic capital allocation; a widening elite critique of its metrics is a leading indicator for where mission-driven capital and talent migrate next.
insights.quote: The things that can be measured, usually with effective altruism, are often not the things that I think are most important in life.

themes.theme: Contagion cycles, vibe shifts, and the limits of pessimism

insights.claim: Burgis argues negative contagion and pessimism cannot compound indefinitely because societies have cultural release valves — vibe shifts and the scapegoat mechanism — that mean-revert sentiment, sometimes overcorrecting.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A structural argument for sentiment mean-reversion and overshoot: extreme pessimism regimes are self-terminating, and the correction tends to overshoot, which is the shape of a contrarian sentiment trade.
insights.quote: The negative contagion and pessimism can’t go on forever.

insights.claim: Burgis expects the current age of pessimism to get worse before it improves, and says it may take something traumatic — a serious war worse than current ones — to give people something to build around.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A near-term-worse, longer-term-better sentiment path with tail risk attached; frames optimism as arising out of tragedy rather than gradual improvement.
insights.quote: I think it might get worse before it gets better.

insights.claim: Burgis predicts the pope's forthcoming AI encyclical will be broadly optimistic about what AI can do for humanity, and says his pro-tech accelerationist friends who expect a crackdown are 'absolutely wrong.'
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable call against a specific consensus in tech circles; a positive encyclical would remove a perceived global-moral-authority overhang on AI narrative risk.
insights.quote: I think he’s going to be very optimistic about what AI can do for humanity, of course, with some cautions about the way that it develops.

insights.claim: Burgis attributes distinctive Anglo and especially American unhappiness to Byung-Chul Han's 'achievement subject' — an internalized Calvinist compulsion toward endless doing that has shaped entrepreneurship, media, and business culture and coincides with the fertility decline.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Names a cultural mechanism behind falling household formation and burnout — inputs to long-horizon demographic, consumer, and labor-supply forecasts, and to demand for anti-burnout products and slower-living geographies.
insights.quote: We’ve internalized this idea that we always have to be doing something. There is always more to achieve.

themes.theme: Algorithmic sorting and the male-female divergence

insights.claim: Burgis blames technology's sorting of what it thinks men versus women should see for widening political and aesthetic polarization specifically between the genders, on top of general polarization.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Frames gender-divergent feeds as a mechanism, not just a symptom — relevant to platform regulatory risk and to the durability of gender-segmented consumer and media markets.
insights.quote: I think technology is largely to blame for that, the way that it sorts things that it thinks men should see versus things that women should see.

insights.claim: Burgis says people now sort on stated preferences before ever meeting a real person of the opposite sex, and notes he would never have found the woman he married via a dating app.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A structural critique of preference-based matching that lines up with widely reported dating-app user dissatisfaction — a headwind for app-based matching models and an opening for in-person and serendipity-based formats.

insights.claim: Burgis reports that roughly 90 percent of the men in his university class watch pornography, with women somewhat lower, and says raising it in class prompts a steady stream of students to seek him out privately.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A first-hand penetration estimate in a young cohort, and evidence of latent unmet demand for intervention — the kind of taboo-plus-ubiquity setup that precedes regulatory action and new friction-introducing products.
insights.quote: the data are something like 90 percent of the men in my class are watching porn, and not quite that number with the women

insights.claim: Burgis's single most-wanted norm change is that young men lose interest in pornography, and he favors deliberately introducing friction into how easily it is found, citing a Free Press story about a 13-year-old girl encountering it accidentally.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Elite-adjacent support for friction and age-gating is a leading indicator of age-verification and content-access regulation, which raises compliance costs for platforms and creates a market for verification infrastructure.
insights.quote: I’m actually relatively in favor of introducing friction into the process and how easy that stuff can be found.

insights.claim: Burgis says Rod Dreher's Benedict Option is right that every family will have to take specific protective actions and put boundaries between children and the broader culture, while rejecting any prescriptive version — he notes Montana has great internet, so relocation solves nothing.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Physical withdrawal no longer works as a filter, so demand shifts to digital boundary-setting products — device controls, filtered networks, schooling choices — rather than geography.
insights.quote: They have great internet in Montana.

themes.theme: False contrarianism and the mimetics of being anti-mimetic

insights.claim: Burgis concedes that mimetic theory itself became a mimetic fad and says René Girard would be 'relatively mortified' by its popularity, which was a running joke in his Stanford circle while he was alive.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: The framework most used to explain herding in Silicon Valley is itself a herding artifact — a caution against treating Girardian language in pitch decks and theses as evidence of independent thinking.
insights.quote: I think Girard would be relatively mortified that mimetic theory was very mimetic and so popular.

insights.claim: Burgis rejects the reading of his book as a call to become the rugged individualist 'one,' arguing the focus has swung too far toward the one and that the real challenge is the relationship between the one and the ninety-nine.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Reframes the founder-genius / lone-contrarian archetype as an overcrowded position, pointing instead to group-self dynamics — useful when assessing whether 'contrarian' positioning is real differentiation or consensus in costume.
insights.quote: I think the focus has actually swung way too far in the direction of the one.

insights.claim: Burgis reads the Gnostic gospel of Thomas version of the lost sheep — where the one lost sheep is the smartest sheep, praised for leaving the herd rather than returned to it — as the interpretation modern audiences find more attractive than the traditional one.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A crisp diagnostic for how 'leave the herd, you're the smart one' narratives sell — the emotional engine behind contrarian newsletters, alt-asset marketing, and exit-the-system pitches.
insights.quote: people would be more attracted to the Gnostic interpretation than the traditional one

insights.claim: Burgis warns that big explanatory ideas become harmful when turned into theories of everything, and cites the claim that reading Girard ruins novelists because they conclude no idea is original — with the antidote being to stop applying the frame and return to particulars.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Cowen explicitly analogizes this to efficient markets theory — a true framework can still be corrosive to hold, a live risk for investors who over-apply a single explanatory model.
insights.quote: It’s a little bit like efficient markets theory. Even if it’s true, it’s better not to believe it?

insights.claim: Burgis says we live in a relatively Manichean society with a dangerous desire for purity, and that every time in his life he tried to flee the messy world he ended up less happy.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Argues that purity-driven sorting — political, ideological, or communal — is a losing strategy; applies directly to the clustering of investors and firms into ideologically homogeneous networks.
insights.quote: There’s a desire for purity. I think the desire for purity is relatively dangerous.

themes.theme: Institution-building: Cluny, third places, and religion in Silicon Valley

insights.claim: Burgis describes the Cluny Institute as a talent network, artist colony, and workshop for people open to the transcendent, and says he is betting it will be building some of the world's most important things — companies, cultural forms, and new institutions — in 10 or 20 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: An explicitly long-duration talent-network bet with a scouting ('bat signal') acquisition model — the same structure as early-stage venture, applied to a religiously-inflected founder pool.
insights.quote: I’m betting that if we can begin to find that network, and invest in that talent network, that 10 or 20 years from now, it will be building some of the most important things in the world.

insights.claim: Burgis argues Silicon Valley would be healthier if it were less allergic to religious thinking, and wants to work at the intersection of Athens, Jerusalem, and Silicon Valley rather than keeping those siloed.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Part of a visible trend of religious sensibility re-entering tech elite circles; relevant to founder-network formation, recruiting narratives, and where mission-aligned LP capital may cluster.
insights.quote: I think religious thinking could do Silicon Valley a lot of good.

insights.claim: Burgis says San Francisco remains the most important city in the world, particularly because of the AI boom, precisely because its cluster has never been replicated anywhere else.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A non-tech-insider endorsement of agglomeration durability — argues against the thesis that AI talent and capital meaningfully disperse to rival hubs, with implications for Bay Area real estate and hiring.
insights.quote: San Francisco is still the most important city in the world, particularly because of the AI boom, because it’s never been replicated anywhere else.

insights.claim: Burgis says his one policy change as dictator would be publicly funding entrepreneurial musicians to open jazz clubs in every US city over 100,000 people, on the theory that America lacks mediating institutions and third places between the individual and the state.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A deficit-of-third-places diagnosis from someone who studies social dynamics; supports demand theses for in-person venue, hospitality, and community-format businesses as substitutes for online affiliation.
insights.quote: I would give them startup funds to open jazz clubs in every single city, and I would fund them from my government.

insights.claim: Burgis holds up the original Cluny as an institutional-design precedent: its founding donor renounced all right to influence its operation, and it grew into a network of over 1,200 monasteries that drove architectural, agricultural, and winemaking innovation for 300 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A concrete historical model for donor-independence governance and franchised networked institutions — directly relevant to how modern foundations, research labs, and endowments structure control.
insights.quote: Its original charter, the guy that gave all of the money renounced his right to have anything to do with the way that it operated.

insights.claim: Burgis says how frequently a Catholic parish offers confession is his number-one predictive signal — parishes that offer it daily or several times a week see lines form, and from that single variable plus adoration frequency he can predict ten other things about the church.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A clean example of a supply-creates-demand signal and of correlated-attribute clustering — the same logic as using one high-information operating metric to infer an organization's whole posture, which he explicitly compares to predicting politics from a gun-control position.
insights.quote: That is the number one signal for me, and then how often they have adoration.

insights.claim: Burgis warns the church has become highly mimetic with the world — priests operating as TikTok influencers performing skits — and argues this destroys the otherworldliness and alterity that Eastern Orthodox liturgy preserves better than the Novus Ordo.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A differentiation argument with general application: institutions that converge on the dominant medium's format forfeit the scarcity that made them valuable — the brand-dilution risk of chasing platform distribution.
insights.quote: I think it’s incredibly unhelpful because there needs to be a level of otherworldliness, alterity

insights.claim: Burgis observes Italy has become formally nonreligious while remaining culturally Catholic — Italians who cross themselves at an ambulance or a street-corner Madonna but have not attended mass in years — and attributes it to fatigue and a failure of intergenerational transmission.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A case study in how brand equity persists long after practice collapses — and how a generation of non-transmission, not sudden rejection, is what actually breaks an institution's base.
insights.quote: It seems like they’re almost tired of their Catholicism. They’ve had it for so long.

insights.claim: Burgis says exorcists appear to be on the rise from anecdotal evidence, notes the church tracks them but does not release the data publicly, and predicts he would not be surprised by a major Marian apparition in his lifetime.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A marker of rising appetite for enchantment and the supernatural — the same demand Cowen links to the UAP discourse — which tends to show up commercially in spirituality, wellness, and mystery-adjacent media.
insights.quote: I’ve known my fair share of exorcists, and they seem to be on the rise, by the way, from what the data shows. Most of it’s anecdotal.

insights.claim: Burgis says he has been totally shocked and scandalized by the surge of mimetic antisemitism on the political right, names Nick Fuentes as incredibly influential with a younger generation, and hopes it is a contagion people will snap out of once exposed.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Treats a fast-moving political shift as a contagion with a possible reversal point rather than a stable realignment — relevant to anyone modeling the durability of the current right-wing coalition.
insights.quote: there is some crazy mimetic thing happening right now. It’s cool to be edgy or something like that

insights.claim: Burgis says he is hosting a conference this summer where Bryan Johnson of the live-forever campaign speaks immediately before a Benedictine monk whose tradition meditates daily on death, and that he keeps a brightly painted Mexican skull on his desk as memento mori.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A crisp framing of the longevity industry's cultural competition: the live-forever thesis versus a memento mori tradition, staged deliberately against each other — the narrative battleground for the sector's mainstream acceptance.

insights.claim: Burgis says he could not name anyone who has died publicly since John Paul II until Ben Sasse, and draws on C. S. Lewis's line about dying a series of small deaths to the ego before dying.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Public dying as a rare, high-salience cultural event is itself becoming a contagion vector for the memento mori revival Burgis is programming around.

themes.theme: Wall Street lessons, careers, and the escape trade

insights.claim: Burgis says his main takeaway from under two years on Wall Street as an investment-banking analyst was that efficient markets theory is BS, and that the material from a good undergraduate business school was not actually used day to day.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A first-hand rejection of EMH from someone who then built a career on mimetic herding — the two views reinforce each other and underwrite an active, behavioral view of price formation.
insights.quote: I learned that efficient markets theory is BS.

insights.claim: Burgis says that as an analyst building pitch decks and Excel models he never got to seek alpha, and speculates he would have been enthralled had he been at a hedge fund instead — he left within two years to start his first company.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Illustrates the persistent talent-retention gap between banking and buy-side/founder paths — the seat, not the industry, determines whether analytical talent stays.
insights.quote: If I had worked at a hedge fund, I would have been enthralled by seeking alpha.

insights.claim: Burgis recounts a senior banker talking him out of his gung-ho pitch to work 80-hour weeks and sleep in the office at Goldman Sachs, and says he dismissed the man as unambitious and unlikely to make it — advice he now thinks was right.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A vivid illustration of the achievement-subject dynamic operating as a recruiting funnel in finance, and of why burnout critiques land only after the fact.
insights.quote: If I can come work at Goldman Sachs, I’ll work 80-hour weeks, I’ll sleep in the office.

insights.claim: Burgis says being an entrepreneur is uniquely difficult because nobody ever tells you to stop and there is always something else to do, and that stepping off operations onto a board while in seminary in Italy was what restored balance.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Names the absence of an external stopping rule as the structural hazard in founder burnout — an argument for governance and board structures that impose one.
insights.quote: Being an entrepreneur is incredibly difficult because nobody ever tells you to stop, and there’s always something else to do.

insights.claim: Burgis's stated escape fantasy is explicit geographic arbitrage — moving his family to Genoa, earning his US income while living in Italy, and working less.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: The US-income/low-cost-Europe trade is now the default fantasy of high-earning American knowledge workers — a demand driver for Italian residency visas, secondary-city property, and cross-border tax services.
insights.quote: It is moving to Genoa with my family, making my US income, living in Italy.

insights.claim: Burgis and Cowen both call Genoa the most underrated city in Italy and Naples their second favorite, noting almost no one they know who visits Italy goes to Genoa and that Naples is dismissed as too dirty.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Two well-traveled tastemakers flagging the same under-visited destinations is exactly the setup that precedes tourism inflows and property repricing in Italian secondary cities.
insights.quote: I think it’s the most underrated city in Italy.

insights.claim: Burgis says Italy, despite its economic stagnation, produces people who seem more joyful and optimistic than Americans he knows who are doing well, and asks whether the stagnant economy has something right that GDP misses.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to using output growth as a proxy for welfare, and part of the same critique he levels at effective altruism's measurement bias.
insights.quote: For all of the economic stagnation and problems that Italy has, do they also have something right?

insights.claim: Burgis says he deliberately stops publicizing Michigan because Northern Michigan and the Traverse City area are getting written up in the New York Times and prices are totally out of control.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: A textbook discovery-to-repricing cycle in second-home real estate: legacy-media coverage is the trigger, and the local price move is already, in his account, well past reasonable.
insights.quote: Northern Michigan, like the Traverse City area, is getting written up in the New York Times, which I hate to see anytime I see it, because it is wonderful. Prices are totally out of control

insights.claim: Burgis argues Northern Italy is less mimetic than the South because the flamboyant, animated, spectacle-oriented disposition of Naples is itself the more contagious mode, while Cowen suggests Italy has fewer status dimensions than America overall.
insights.speaker: Luke Burgis
insights.so_what: Frames the number of available status dimensions as a variable that differs by culture — a way to think about which consumer markets support endless product differentiation and which converge on a few canonical goods.
